newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-BRAZILIAN SOCCER CUPS CONFUSE AND CONFOUND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BRAZILIAN SOCCER CUPS CONFUSE AND CONFOUND.

text.p: The weird and wonderful formats used to organise Brazil's soccer tournaments continue to confuse and confound players and fans alike.
None of the 15 players interviewed by a newspaper this week fully understood the rules of the Rio de Janeiro championship in which they are playing.
O Globo said each player was asked four basic questions about the format and none got all the answers right.
Botafogo, already guaranteed a place in the final play-off, were bemused to find they will be penalised simply because they were the first team to qualify.

But while some teams scratch their heads over the rules, others are twiddling their thumbs. Four have already been eliminated from the competition after playing just 11 times and have a four-month wait for their next competitive match.
The Rio championship has been divided into three stages with the winners of each qualifying for the decisive stage. Botafogo won the first and the second has just started.
So far, so good. But what happens if one team wins two stages. And if three teams each win one stage, does anyone have an advantage in the final round?
In the first case, two teams will contest a three-match final in which the double-stage winners need only two draws or one win in three games to take the title.

Botafogo were astounded to discover that the answer to the second question was that they lose out every time. If Botafogo finish the play-off tournament level on points with the winners of the second or third stage, their opponents take the title automatically.

If there is a three-way tie, the winners are the team with the best overall record in the tournament -- provided they won the second or third stage. The first stage winners are automatically out of the running.
Yet the first stage is the hardest to win. The 12 teams met each other once and the top two then played off to decide the winners.

This meant Botafogo had to play a final, despite winning all 11 matches and finishing eight points ahead of Vasco da Gama. "In any other country in the world, we would have been champions without this game," said central defender Goncalves.

Only the top eight in the first stage go into the second stage and only the top six in the second stage qualify for the third. This means the second stage winners only are the best over seven games and the third stage are the best over five.

Eduardo Viana, president of the Rio federation, blamed the clubs, who decide on the format. "It's incoherent but they wanted it this way," he said, explaining that Flamengo, Botafogo and Fluminense wanted to devalue the first stage because it coincided with a more lucrative Rio-Sao Paulo Cup.
The rules are even harder on the teams knocked out in the first round.
America, one of the unlucky sides, are now training hard for their next game -- which will be in August when the third divison of the Brazilian championship gets under way.
"I'm afraid of being forgotten," said goalkeeper Emerson, who gave some good performances in the team's brief campaign. "By the time this competition finishes, nobody will remember us."
The rules of the Sao Paulo championship have also caused perplexity.

In this tournament, the 16 teams are divided into two groups. They then play once against the teams in their own group and twice against the teams in the other group. The top two then qualify from each group.
Critics say this means teams play a sequence of fixtures against opponents with whom they are not in direct competition.
More bizarre still is that Palmeiras in group one and Sao Paulo and Corinthians in group two are considered to be in a different class to the other teams.
This means 23 rounds of eight fixtures are played -- simply to decide who joins Palmeiras, Sao Paulo and Corinthians in the finals.
